subtopic: POST OFFICE CONSTRUCTION-STATEMENT ON WINTER PROGRAM

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public
Works): I wish to report to the house on an important part of my department's program for winter work. A total of 64 small post office buildings are being erected across Canada this winter. The program is now well under way, and the buildings are all part of the government's regular accommodation requirements. Construction was deferred wherever possible during the summer so that they might form part of the program for winter work.
The policy of erecting small, standard plan post offices during the winter months was inaugurated during 1958-59 and, with the completion of this winter's program, a total of 259 such structures will have been built under this scheme in the smaller communities of Canada. Each building provides between 600 and 800 square feet of working space and costs not more than $25,000, including land. In all cases tenders have been called locally to permit the use of local workers who may be unemployed during the winter months.
This winter's program is proceeding at a satisfactory pace, and wherever possible the work will be completed by March 31. To date tenders have been called or contracts awarded for 56 post offices. In a few of the communities listed buildings may not be erected as planned, but such instances are expected to be extremely rare.
The construction of standard plan post offices constitutes only a part of the over-all winter works program carried out by the Department of Public Works. For a number of years it has been standard practice to defer certain types of work from the summer and to let the contracts at such a time as to provide the maximum amount of winter work. In addition building contracts, both large and small, continue to carry a clause which specifies that work must not be stopped during the winter months without the express permission of the department.
A list of the communities where new post offices are planned follows, and I would ask, without reading it, to have it form part of Hansard.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ONTARIO-REPORTED INTENTION TO REMOVE LOGGING TAX
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Finance a question occasioned by Premier Robarts' statement yesterday that the logging and pulp and paper industries could expect an early announcement regarding the removal of the logging tax. Has the minister taken under consideration in 1962 any representations from the Ontario government to end the dual nature of the taxation on the logging industry in Ontario?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ONTARIO-REPORTED INTENTION TO REMOVE LOGGING TAX
speechtext:
I have not seen the statement attributed by the hon. member to Premier Robarts. He was evidently referring to the provincial logging tax. As far as the federal government is concerned, the reference is to the federal income tax imposed on companies engaged in this area of endeavour.

This subject was discussed at the last dominion-provincial conference and there has been continuing discussion of it between the federal government and governments at the provincial level, particularly of those provinces which have a more direct concern. I arranged several weeks ago for a conference to be held at the official level to examine the subject further, a conference to which the provinces were invited and to which the industry was also invited to send representatives. A date was tentatively proposed, but the officials of the government of British Columbia indicated that they were not in a position to attend at that time. We have asked them to suggest some later date in order that the proposed conference may proceed.

subtopic: ONTARIO-REPORTED INTENTION TO REMOVE LOGGING TAX
speechtext:
Can the minister indicate
whether there is going to be a bilateral announcement, a statement not only by Mr. Robarts but by himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ONTARIO-REPORTED INTENTION TO REMOVE LOGGING TAX
speechtext: I do not understand what the hon. member means by "announcement".

subtopic: ONTARIO-REPORTED INTENTION TO REMOVE LOGGING TAX
speechtext: My question is this. Premier Robarts has indicated an early announcement. Is the minister prepared to indicate whether he is going to be sharing that announcement with Premier Robarts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ONTARIO-REPORTED INTENTION TO REMOVE LOGGING TAX
speechtext:
There is no particular announcement, Mr. Speaker. It is within the power of the premier of the province to make a comment whenever he thinks it proper concerning the provincial logging tax. That is, after all, a provincial tax. As to the federal tax, I do not contemplate any announcement.
I hope this conference can be held soon. I hope the province of British Columbia will be able to be represented at it on the official level and that we can have fruitful discussions, because it is a matter that requires a joint approach on the part of both the federal and provincial levels of government. The whole question relates to the tax position of this industry in respect of both federal and provincial taxation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Has the minister any comment to make concerning the warning voiced by the United States under secretary of the treasury, reported in today's Gazette under the headline "Dollar Continues Lower Despite Fund Support", against manipulation of the exchange rate-to quote the article-"through which one country or another can seek temporary refuge

Inquiries of the Ministry from balance of payments disciplines by juggling its exchange rate-beggaring its neighbors-"?

maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext: Question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext: Order. The minister may wish to comment, but may I point out that what the hon. member has done is to read a report of something that took place outside the country and ask the minister whether he wishes to comment on it. I have no doubt that a question could be asked about a matter of that kind; therefore I do not propose to declare the question out of order. I am, however, attempting to suggest to hon. members that when a public issue arises which they consider to be a matter of urgency and of the administrative responsibilities of a minister it ought to be framed as a specific question for information and not merely as an invitation to comment.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with great respect, on the point you raised, yesterday a question was asked by an hon. member on the government side of the house inviting the Prime Minister to comment on a statement made by a United States senator. That was considered, I gather, quite in order and comment was made at some length. Certainly that is parallel to the question just asked.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext: I may be in error about this, but my point is that it seems to me if we were to allow questions on statements made around the world on various matters in the form "would the minister care to comment", it would open the door to unlimited inquiry; but where the subject matter is something that falls within the administrative responsibilities of the minister-and the exchange rate does, of course, in the present instance-and if it is an urgent matter it may be brought before the house as the basis of a question. My intervention is in the interest of seeing that questions are asked as questions seeking specific information and not general invitations to comment on what other people say.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may treat the question as one relating to the subject matter of the exchange rate rather than as being asked to comment on something that has been attributed to someone else in the press, J would be glad to comment on the subject matter of the exchange rate and the steps the government has been taking in that regard.
It is not fair to call the Canadian rate a manipulated rate. That, I think, is an opprobrious term, and it is quite unfair. The policy the government has followed in regard to the exchange rate and the external 26207-1-46J
value of the Canadian dollar is well known, and we have made known month by month the extent of the net transactions of the month through the foreign exchange fund in purchases and sales.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that since June 20, 1961, the date of the last budget when the present policy was announced, the exchange value of the Canadian dollar has moved within a narrow range, and the operations of our exchange fund on each side of the market have approximately balanced out. At the close of business on January 31- these figures will be announced in the regular course today-our official holdings of gold and United States dollars were $1,922 million. At the end of May, 1961, the last publication date before the June budget, our holdings were $1,949 million. Thus, apart from the sum of $50 million which we lent from our reserves in August and September as part of a general move to provide support for sterling, our reserves at the end of last month were within $25 million of where they stood shortly before the budget.
While there have been periods, such as in October and January, when our exchange fund has operated extensively, it has not operated in an aggressive manner; that is to say, it has not driven the rate in one direction or another. On the contrary, it has at all times responded to and moderated market pressures.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this statement will put an end to the kind of talk we have heard about a manipulated exchange rate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Does the minister deny that the government intervenes from time to time in order to influence the rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. COMMENT ON EXCHANGE RATE
speechtext: I think the hon. member will find the answer to his question and some additional information in the answer I have just given, when he has an opportunity to consider it. I have said that where the exchange fund has operated it has not operated aggressively. It has not driven the rate in one direction or another. On the contrary, it has at all times responded to and moderated market pressures.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, February 8, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Monteith (Perth)- Mr. Martineau in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Disabled Persons Act to increase to sixty five dollars per month the maximum amount of allowance in respect of which payments may be made to the provinces under the provisions of that act, and to increase the total amount of allowable income, inclusive of allowance, by one hundred and eighty dollars a year in the case of an unmarried person and three hundred and sixty dollars a year in the case of a married person.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE PAYMENTS AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words on this disability pension program, Mr. Chairman, and I wish to do so clear of the garbage that appeared to be thrown into this discussion yesterday in the form of election proposals. I faintly heard an interjection by an hon. member, and if he wishes to repeat it I shall be happy to take up the argument that was taking place yesterday. If he does not wish to do so, that suits me fine, because I should like to discuss the disability pension itself.
I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton South who yesterday pointed out that disability pensions were very important, in that the recipient received more than just a subsistence allowance. In many cases the receipt of this pension enables the disabled person to take his place in the community when he would otherwise be dependant on his family
Disabled Persons Act
or on the community. This pension does allow those over 18 years of age to qualify to take their place in the community. I suggest that this possibility might be further extended if the minister could give consideration to some of the limitations connected with this particular pension.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in order to qualify for a disability pension one must prove that he is totally and permanently disabled. This means, in ordinary language, that the person must have one foot in the grave and the other one must be very close to it without any chance of recovery. I believe this fact limits the extent to which this pension could apply, and limits the social advantages that might be derived from the pension if the restrictions were not so stringent. I believe that some people who are suffering from cancer, and who are incapable of working, should be able to qualify for this pension. It is true that in some cases there is a possibility of recovery, but this sometimes turns out to be merely a hope rather than a fact. Such people might derive some advantage from this pension.
The same situation applies to people who are suffering from arthritis and rheumatism. While it is true there may be a cure for arthritis and rheumatism, the damage done to the patient by the disease often means he is totally incapacitated after the disease has been arrested. I can only speak of the province of Ontario, but the clause in the act relating to the totally and permanently disabled means that many people who should be able to obtain this pension are denied its benefits. I think the minister should give consideration to amending this particular clause, because in my opinion it has worked a hardship in a number of cases.
Yesterday we heard a great deal about social justice and this so-called social security scheme. Another limiting factor in connection with this particular pension is the situation where a man may be totally and permanently disabled and would be able to qualify for the pension except for the fact that his wife has a job. In this case it is impossible for him to obtain this type of assistance. I cannot for the life of me see what difference it makes whether or not a man's wife has the initiative and ability to go out and work in so far as his receipt of the disability pension is concerned. Certainly, according to our legal interpretation of dependency, it has not been necessary for a wife to support a husband. There have been some cases of disagreement as to whether or not the rule should work the other way and the husband should have to support his wife. Certainly it has not worked in reverse.

Disabled Persons Act
In this connection I should like to cite a letter I received, which says in view of the fact that Mrs.-I shall not use the name- is employed, the income may be in excess of the ceiling imposed by the act for a married applicant. In this particular case the man has no job. He is bedridden as a result of arthritis, but his wife has a job in the telephone exchange. She is doing what she can to keep the household together. It is a fact that if she were to stop working tomorrow the husband could qualify for this pension, but he certainly could not keep his wife on $55 a month or even the $65 he will receive after this amendment. His wife will have to continue to work, which means that this man is dependant on his wife for his very existence, and this fact is known in the community.
I feel this situation is damaging to the morale of those people who are disabled, because if they could obtain the pension they could take their position in the community without being dependant on their wives for their daily bread. I do not believe the income earned by the family jointly, or by the wife, should be considered as income of the husband who is making application for a disability pension. His disability should be sufficient to enable him to qualify. The wife cannot stop working, because the family has to be supported. There is no additional allowance given to the wife, and I think this is a limiting factor which should be eliminated at the suggestion of the federal government.
The minister spoke about setting up a welfare council. One of the duties of this welfare council no doubt will be to consider the means by which we can reintroduce disabled persons into a useful life. I am sure everyone will agree that if we could pay the disability pension it would help a disabled person to take his place in the community without being dependant on the community. I think the people are truly desirous of having these disabled people return to work. However, it has come to my attention that the ceiling on income is so low that a disabled person cannot possibly be employed without losing his pension.
I shall give a particular example of a person who is disabled. He is not so bright mentally as some people, but I do not imagine he would be classed in the lowest bracket of mental advancement. He applied for a job in a bicycle shop where there was an opening for a man to fix tires and repair bicycles during the season when that is applicable in northern Ontario. The job could not have lasted more than six months. The man who employed him has been employing disabled people for a number of years.

He is very sympathetic toward them and has even employed disabled persons who have to use wheel chairs. In some cases the people he has employed were considered unemployable for many years.
In the particular case which I refer the disabled man asked for $12 a week, and the employer said he would not pay him $12 a week as he did not consider it sufficient. He said he would hire him on a temporary basis and pay him $25 a week, which was the minimum he considered proper on grounds of public opinion and for other reasons. I should state that the employee first established his disability pension in 1956, and he was employed in the bicycle shop from May 8, 1961 to September 20, 1961. Then, before he was laid off, an investigator came to him and said "By such and such a date you will have earned so much money that you will be over the $750 allowed; therefore we will have to get back an overpayment of $110 from you".
Now, Mr. Chairman, that may be true. The act says that a person is not allowed to make over $750 but I feel this man could have been employed for a year at less than $750, or employed for six months and allowed to earn the $750. However, the department took away his disability pension and instigated an action against him to get back the overpayment of $110. They left the man without his disability pension and without a job, and he is now on municipal relief receiving $46.35 a month. If on $55 a month he could not pay back the $110, how in thunder do they expect him to pay it back on the $46 which he receives in municipal welfare?
I do not particularly want to pursue this case, except to say that the employer also hired a person in a wheel chair who was afflicted with arthritis. The employer taught him how to keep books and established him as an accountant. This man had not worked for over 20 years, but when this employer hired him he worked in the plant for a number of years until he finally broke his neck by falling out of his wheel chair. That man told me that the mere fact he was able to get the job meant for him the difference between wanting to live and not wanting to live. It was not the money that was his sole concern, it was the fact that somebody would give him a job.
I believe this employer should be commended for his efforts in trying to rehabilitate disabled persons, but as long as we maintain a ceiling on earnings which makes it impossible for that employer to pay even a minimum wage, then he is going to be very sceptical about employing others. In

fact he has said that he will not employ disabled people any longer in any of his shops, for the sole reason that he does not want to get into the position of being accused of helping them to lose their disability pensions. In the case I mentioned, the fact that he paid the employee more than the minimum meant that the man lost his pension. I suppose his pension can be re-established, but to me it seems very unfair and I believe the provisions of the act should take into consideration the wage that would be paid under the minimum wage act.
If this employee were a woman in Ontario the minimum wage law would apply, and an employer could not pay an amount of money which would permit the employee to remain at work and still receive the minimum wage. There are certain jobs which a person's mental capacity will allow him to do, and I believe this should be a consideration of the government.
Certainly every disabled person in the country appreciates the fact that this additional $10 will be paid, but I believe that the minister, if he really believes in social justice, about which we have been hearing so much, should consider allowing an increase in the ceiling upon earnings of people in receipt of disability pension. This is very important and has been important in regard to other pensions. The minister can turn to his colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and he will find that department has done a great deal in relation to the employment of people who are receiving total disability pensions under the veterans affairs legislation. That department has felt that even though a person is considered to be unemployable he may be able to do certain types of work.
I should now like to refer to one person for whom people in northern Ontario have a great deal of respect because of the courage she shows. She is a young lady who often appears on television programs in the town of North Bay. She is badly crippled by arthritis and rheumatism. She can hardly get around, yet she has been able to conduct a program on television and has been able to impart to others some of her own cheerfulness and vivacity. Her courage is obvious to those who know of her disability, and she has been able to give a great deal of encouragement to all those who are similarly afflicted in that area.
I am not aware what her earnings are, but if they appear to be more than would be allowed by the department, consideration should be given to the problem. That is one very exceptional case, and I believe that in this and similar cases the earnings limit of $750 should be removed. As members in the
Disabled Persons Act
House of Commons well know, there are those in our ranks who are disabled, and it is my contention that disabled persons should at least be allowed the opportunity to become fully employed, even at the minimum amount of money, because of the rehabilitation effect which employment has on them. The minister may not be prepared to do it today, but I hope that in the very near future he will give consideration to removing the ceiling, and also the regulation that makes it necessary for a wife's income to be considered in giving to the head of the household a disability pension on his own behalf.
I hope the minister will give consideration to these matters, and will also review the clause that demands that a person be totally and permanently disabled. I say this because many of our citizens are in a position now to expect and demand assistance but their doctors cannot certify that there will not be a new medical discovery tomorrow that will make it possible for them to recover at least to a partial extent. The minister is giving consideration to this matter; he has mentioned that he has set up a council that will discuss these things. I hope he will take these questions into consideration when the subject is raised again for discussion.

Mr. Chairman, may I draw an anomaly to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare who has put this resolution before us. It concerns people who may be in hospitals or public institutions and who are disabled persons within the meaning of the act, yet there is a disparity between their right to this allowance as compared with old age assistance or assistance to blind people who are perhaps under similar conditions in these institutions.
The anomaly is this. While the payments may contine under the Old Age Assistance Act and to blind persons, under certain circumstances these payments are not made under the disabled persons allowances act. This was recently considered at some length at a meeting in Truro, Nova Scotia, of the municipal home superintendents and matrons of that province. I do not want to take up the time of the committee unduly, but the sections of the act which create the problem are sections 21 and 22. Section 21 says that subject to section 22 an allowance shall not be paid during the period that a recipient is a patient or a resident in a hospital, nursing home, infirmary, home for the aged, an institution for the care of incurables, or a private charitable or public institution.
Then section 22 sets out certain conditions under which the payments may be made, but it is not a blanket form of payment available to all disabled people who find themselves in

Disabled Persons Act
the institutions I have mentioned. This seems to me to be an anomaly which creates a certain bitterness, or at least dissatisfaction. A disabled person feels that his plight is at least as serious as that of a person who is blind or a person who requires old age assistance. My suggestion-while the resolution does not specifically cover this-is that this anomaly should be considered by the new national council on welfare which will be established.
There is another point I should like to make. I am sorry I did not have an opportunity to make it last night when that paragon of perpetual attendance in the House of Commons, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, was here. He is not here this morning. I was interested to note that in his lengthy discourse at no time did he mention disabled persons, although this was the subject of the debate before us. I had occasion previously to say that 90 per cent of his compassion was directed to the old Liberal party and 10 per cent to those in need. I would say that last night he reached 100 per cent compassion for his party.
Perhaps he has been communing with the premier of Newfoundland, who must also have been dissatisfied that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate seems to have transferred his affections to the premier of Quebec. No doubt this will be righted and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate told where his benefaction does come from.

If the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was not in order he had two excellent precedents, one set by the minister who introduced the resolution and the other by the Prime Minister himself.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister a question about something which has always bothered me in connection with this legislation. We are initiating here a measure which will apply to disabled persons all across Canada from St. John's to Vancouver. The hon. member for Timiskaming has already pointed out that there is one problem in connection with this matter, which is that to qualify for this pension a person must be considered to be permanently disabled.
It is very difficult, in the light of advances in today's medicine, for anyone to determine when a person is permanently disabled. I think the federal government should modify this requirement in the light of scientific advances in medicine, and make it applicable to a person who has been disabled for a certain length of time. I say this because a person has to eat whether he is disabled for one year or for the rest of his life, and the purpose of this legislation is to help people who are in need; it is to take care of their need. I suggest that this measure should be adjusted to make the need the governing factor in the administration of this legislation.
The second problem that bothers me, and the second question I wish to put to the minister, is this. This legislation is administered by the provinces, and in particulai it is administered by boards set up under the auspices of the provincial health departments. This means that we have ten separate boards in Canada from St. John's to Vancouver, one for each province. How, then, do we ensure that a person in St. John's gets exactly the same treatment as a person in Vancouver? What criteria, if any, are we setting up for the guidance of these boards in order to avoid disparities in cases of this kind? I have the uncomfortable feeling that a person can qualify for benefit under this act in one province whereas, though he might be suffering from exactly the same condition, he would be disqualified in another. I think that is something we should seek to remedy, and I ask the minister when he replies to tell us what we are doing along these lines.

speechtext:
Yesterday we had an example in this matter, which might have taken a very short while, of the minister and the Prime Minister both making a real effort to introduce into this debate a partisan note that

7X7
perhaps has not been heard this session. The
Prime Minister, indeed, touched on almost everything but the issue before the house. He was like a hockey player who did not care whether his stick touched the puck as long as it touched a lot of other people in the game and even outside the game.
I ask this committee to consider, before we end this debate, whether there can be some responsible reply from the minister as to how this important matter is to be financed. We on our side believe that this amount of additional payment is not adequate. At the same time we believe that an adequate scheme has got to be paid for. There has not yet in the course of this debate, to my knowledge, been any suggestion whatsoever as to how Canada, with record deficits piled up over these past four years, is going to finance this important project.
I submit there is something vulgar, immediately prior to a general election, in using some of the senior people, who have done so much to enable those of us who are younger to start out in life with fine opportunities, as pawns in a political game. Some of these people who will be receiving pensions on account of disability and old age are people who remember paying for things when those things were due.
On our side we have earnestly put forward a scheme which was the result of many months of research by experts, as we believe, and which was to some extent the aftermath of the study of the Clark commission report. But there were many interjections yesterday from the minister, when again and again he asked the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, "What would you cut out?" I do not find these interjections appearing in Hansard, but we remember them. The only possible inference was that if we were going to be responsible and balance the budget we were going to have to cut out some payments; or, alternatively, that the payments could not be made.
I put to the committee that there is an alternative, and the alternative is the theory of growth; the theory that this country can go places, the theory that in the field of social security we have not reached the end of the line by any means that we are, in fact, part of an affluent society and that our capacities in the fields of production, technology, the service industries and so on vastly exceed our consumptive capacity and that as time goes by we are therefore going to be able to provide better living for many people providing that people are not wasting their lives in unemployment and that people's services are used until a reasonable time of life. That
may well be, in the future, to the age of 55 or even younger. Maybe we shall be working a substantially shorter week.
It is only if we have a theory of growth that this will happen. It is time we started thinking in terms of a greatly enlarged productive capacity which would be possible for Canada if we have not this great waste of human resources, the wasted years in Canada. The lack of growth which we have experienced is at the root of many of our problems. I would remind this committee that the Gordon commission report of November, 1956 was a study of Canada's potential as it then appeared to a variety of people across Canada. I think it is fair to speculate that the chairman to that commission, who now appears as politically partisan, and many people who appeared before that commission had no reason to think in November, 1956, and before that, that the then Liberal administration would be defeated. Their prediction was honest, fair and reasonable; yet with respect to all their expectations for these last four years we have failed to reach a reasonable accomplishment. If we think of output in general terms, if we think of the average output per individual, gross national expenditure, personal consumption expenditure, of growth factors, capital formation, of government expenditure, of exports and imports or of consumer expenditure, what do we find? Only in the field of imports have we reached expectations of those years.
In the budget debate of some months ago I raised some questions which to me were relevant to this whole question of where we are going, particularly in connection with this matter which we are debating now. The question at that moment was how we were possibly going to finance the kind of exchange manipulation then contemplated. That is the only word which I think can be attributed to the exchange policy; this has been the expression used by Mr. W. Earle McLaughlin and a number of financial editors who have considered what took place during the last year. I put to the house the proposition that we could pay for this only in one of three ways, either by taxation or by borrowing or by printing.
I put to the committee the same question today. How are we going to pay for this additional expenditure? It is not a contributory plan as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition and by many business experts across the country and many authorities in the United States and Britain. How are we going to pay for this? We have three ways of paying for it, the same three ways; either we tax for it or alternatively we borrow or, third, we print.

Disabled Persons Act
I ask hon. members to consider, when we look at the returns we have had in this house to certain questions-for instance, the return that was given on January 29 with respect to the total currency of chartered bank deposits-whether that is not exactly what this government intends to do, to print for it. We have had no suggestion from the other side as to how they are going to pay for this scheme. I think this is a responsible, urgent and important question. Let us not fail these good people, either disabled or old. The hon. member for Stormont yesterday began to read to the committee a little scripture. May I refer him to the book of Haggai, chapter 1, verse 6:
-and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.
I invite the minister to consider all the implications which may result from simple spiral inflation unless the government is prepared to come to grips with its responsibilities before we go to the country. The government will have to accept reality and take the position of saying, "Yes, there have to be larger payments, and this is where they are coming from".
We cannot anticipate the budget debate in this discussion. However, let me make clear that in the opinion of hon. members on this side of the house these grants are not nearly sufficient to meet the current needs of many people who are caught in the problem of increased living costs, the problems attendant upon urbanization and curtailed employment. I invite the minister's attention to the book of Luke, chapter 14, verse 28:
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Within the next few months the people of Canada must decide in whom they will repose their trust for the crucial five year period ahead. It is important that the government adopt a responsible attitude at this time.
Many people experience difficulty in making application for disability pensions. The pride of some people is such that they have difficulty putting themselves in a position in which it appears to them they are asking for a handout. It is one thing for a man disabled in service to his country during war to receive assistance. He has had the honour of serving in Her Majesty's forces, of wearing the uniform of his country with dignity and pride. But it is another thing for a farmer or workman to have to request assistance. In my constituency I recently had the experience of assisting a man from Belgium who was in financial difficulties and unemployed. He had sent his daughter

to university and was now in the dreadful position of requiring assistance. He was one of the 980-odd unemployed in Brockville now seeking employment. His pride made it difficult for him to accept help. He said he would rather sell his home and go back to the country of his origin where he could secure employment.
I have letters from many disabled people. These are proud individuals who do not wish to beg. The suggestion was made last evening by an hon. member sitting to my right that questions of this nature should be taken out of the realm of politics. I subscribe to that. To play politics with a question of this nature is shameful and disgraceful.
The situation would be made easier for applicants for disability pensions if there were a medical board which could examine the individual and give an expert opinion as to his or her position. The limitations and handicaps of the people should be considered. Sometimes these limitations are internal, psychological and deep rooted. Many disabled Canadians have too much pride and courage, and an inherent sense of dignity to make application because of the implications of so doing. It is an evil and base practice that an aura of politicking should surround situations of this type. There has to be a certain degree of co-operation between provincial and federal representatives in matters of this kind and this co-operation should be on a completely non-political basis.
I have spoken at greater length than I intended. In concluding let me say that we on this side of the house will support this measure although we do not feel it is adequate. We are concerned at the government's failure to meet problems of this type realistically. We disapprove of the government's practice of applying ad hoc solutions to burning social problems. We in the Liberal party feel that Canada enjoys a growing, expanding economy. We feel that Canada has never had as great opportunities as lie before us today if the government would show more concern over policy than politics.
We in this party and the people of Canada would like to know what the government is going to do in this regard. It would appear from the statement made by the minister yesterday and from the remarks of the Prime Minister that the government is still not thinking in terms of Canada's potential for growth and expansion.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Monteith (Perth) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-62, to amend the Disabled Persons Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-55, to amend the Old Age Assistance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there are certain aspects of the amendments now before the house which I believe warrant some further explanation. As hon. members will see from the bill, we are proposing to re-enact section 3(1) of the Old Age Assistance Act to permit an increase of $10 in the monthly maximum payment available to senior citizens in the age groups 65 to 69 who are in need. This increase, as is the case with the existing amount, will be shared on a 50-50 basis by the federal and provincial governments if the latter give their assent to the present amendment.
Changes are also proposed in section 3(2) pertaining to income ceilings allowable in establishing eligibility for old age assistance. As I indicated at the resolution stage, these ceilings are being raised beyond the point
Old Age Assistance Act necessary to permit recipients to benefit fully from the higher maximum pension level. This means, in effect, that recipients will henceforth be in a position to have greater earnings without having their benefits reduced.
I might spend a few moments in outlining the effects of these changes. As the resolution indicated, allowable income ceilings are to be raised by $180 a year in the case of an unmarried recipient and by $360 a year in the case of married couples. For example, an unmarried recipient who is presently allowed to have $960 a year, including assistance, will be permitted a total of $1,140 a year. This will be made up of $780 in assistance payments and $360 in outside income. Under existing provisions the maximum outside income allowable without reduction in assistance is $300, which means that with approval of this amendment a recipient will be able to earn 20 per cent more than at the present time. The thinking behind this increase is, of course, to encourage individual initiative wherever possible so that the higher assistance rate may be supplemented by higher earnings.
In the case of a married couple, the maximum allowable income is now $1,620 a year including assistance. This is to be raised to $1,980 a year. With married couples, one spouse or both may be eligible for assistance. If one is eligible they can, of course, receive $780 by way of assistance but can have as much as $1,200 a year in outside income before there is any reduction in the assistance payable. Under present provisions their outside income is limited to $960. If both spouses are eligible they will be able to receive $1,560 by way of assistance and $420 by way of outside income. Under present provisions their outside income is limited to $300.
In the case where one spouse is blind the income ceilings are higher. Such a couple may in future receive as much as $2,340 a year in total income including assistance as against $1,980 under present provisions. Where one spouse receives old age assistance and the other a blindness allowance they will be able to receive as much as $1,560 a year by way of benefit, and to have in addition as much as $780 a year in outside income. The corresponding figures at present are $1,320 and $660 respectively.
Section 2 provides for an effective date of February 1, 1962, as far as the federal government is concerned. Since the old age assistance program is a joint undertaking with the provinces the latter will, of course, have to come to a decision to implement these changes in their own jurisdiction before the changes can become effective.
To this end, when the resolution preceding introduction of this bill was presented to

Old Age Assistance Act the house I wired each of the provinces informing them of the nature and scope of the proposed changes. Subsequently, when the bill was placed before the house copies of the same were immediately sent out to the provincial governments. We are, of course, hopeful that all will accept the present amendments, and when they do my department will do everything possible to assist in the revision of the agreements which form the basis for old age assistance payments in each province.
Assuming that all 10 provinces and the two territories decide to implement these changes, the added expenditures involved in so far as the federal government is concerned will be of the order of $7.2 million over the next 12 month period. This will bring our total annual outlay for old age assistance to an estimated $37.8 million.
There is one further point. While the lower age limit for this program under existing legislation is 65, there are people who are prematurely aged and also widows and spinsters in the age group 60-64, for example, who may be in circumstances where they need financial assistance. In such cases I would emphasize that although persons in these categories cannot qualify for old age assistance they are eligible for assistance, if in need, through provincial programs in which the federal government shares half the cost under the Unemployment Assistance Act. In this connection I think of recipients under the widows' allowances program in Alberta, who some years ago were brought within the federal-provincial sharing arrangements under the Unemployment Assistance Act. In addition, the recently introduced provisions for widows and spinsters in Quebec provide a further illustration of how this joint measure can be helpful in meeting the cost of payments to these persons who are in need. In other provinces social assistance for widows and spinsters has not been designated as a specific program in provincial legislation in the same manner. But there again social assistance is available to such persons when in need, with the federal government paying half the cost of payments made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ASSISTANCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party will, of course, support this measure which is based on a bill that was introduced by the previous Liberal administration. The increase being proposed is essential. It will help to some extent to compensate for the continuing rise in the cost of living and the continuing rise in municipal, provincial and federal tax levels.
This particular plan of old age assistance arises out of action taken by the government


of Canada in 1950, when the federal government of that day removed the means test for persons over 70. I personally campaigned for this change in 1949 because previous to that time I had come face to face with many people of advanced years who were too proud to seek assistance even though they needed it desperately. To help overcome that situation the universal pension was put into effect in 1950.
At that time, however, it was intended to be a supplement to private savings and it was represented as being a supplement to private savings, but throughout the years it has been given a somewhat different interpretation. It has come to be represented as an amount which in its entirety should, in the view of this parliament, be ample for people to live on. This, of course, was not the original idea, and it is obvious that for most people it is quite inadequate for sustenance unless the person has some other means of support. Newspapermen have attempted to live on the old age pension and have demonstrated its inadequacy as a result of their experience. Of course it is inadequate for people who have no private savings. On the other hand, for people who do have private savings it is in many cases superfluous.
In the process of evolution the whole subject of pensions has become a political auction. I was very much impressed by the speech by the hon. member for Leeds a few minutes ago, who put this matter in perspective. We should not be required to deal in a political way with the lives of the senior citizens of this country. It is a retrograde step, and most unfortunate.
Notwithstanding the changes that are now before us the payments are still not going to be adequate to meet the needs. This was demonstrated by the minister himself when he spoke a few minutes ago. He said there are many widows and spinsters between the ages of 60 and 64 who are not covered by the act. In this regard he explained that in some provinces there are plans in which the federal government co-operates. I think he only mentioned two provinces, which means that in the other eight provinces and the territories there are no plans, either provincial or federal, to assist widows and spinsters between the ages of 60 and 64. The fact is that the gaps in the total program are still great.
The minister has advised that the permissible outside income of the recipient of this assistance will be increased, and this is desirable and welcome. However, the limitations are still such that if the outside income and the old age assistance were the only source of support, then in our metropolitan areas

such as Toronto and Montreal people would still be unable to exist in dignity on the amount of money provided.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that unless there is some more fundamental approach we shall continue with this auction, increasing the permissible income from time to time and increasing the pension a little bit from time to time, without coming to grips with the problem in its entirety. It seems to me that is what has to be done.
We have not been advised by the minister as to how the present plans, including the one before us, are to be financed. This is an important omission. It does not take any great amount of intelligence to spend money. It takes a great degree of intelligence to introduce measures which will get the country growing again in such a fashion that social security measures can be paid for from growth rather than by increases in debt. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the attitude of the present government in this respect can be characterized as that of a second mortgage government. Rather than earning money and then spending that which has been earned, in which case there would be no interest charges to pay, the government spends the money first and has to pay interest on its borrowings. In effect they are paying twice for their expenditures. We believe it is unfortunate that the government should come to this parliament and request measures, desirable though they may be on their own merit, which are not financed from the dynamics of growth which we have come to understand and appreciate in this country in years gone by.
It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come for a comprehensive re-examination of our social security legislation; that the time has come for the introduction of a contributory pension plan which will enable people throughout their earning years to pay in some proportion of their annual income and, as a result, be entitled at the time of retirement to draw a pension adequate to their requirements. Such a plan would apply to widows and spinsters between the ages of 60 and 64 who are now not covered by any federal plan. This plan would also permit a greater variation, greater flexibility, in the age at which people retire, because there is a considerable difference in individual capacity. One person may, because of health or other reasons, find it necessary or desirable to retire at an earlier age than some other person. What we need is a comprehensive plan which is flexible enough to meet individual needs. It must be flexible enough to meet individual needs in such a way that the question of pride, the question of charity is removed, and so that the contributions made by people
Old Age Assistance Act throughout their earning years will entitle them to claim an adequate pension as a matter of right.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we wish that at this time the government had introduced such a plan rather than the amendments which have been placed before us. We think the government were tardy, having had the Clark report before them throughout these years and having promised this plan in the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958, in not preparing one for introduction at this time. The measures which have been introduced are further expedients; they are further ad hoc measures. They do not meet the needs in their entirety. They leave gaping holes in the needs, and they do not meet the objections which have existed in the past such as the fact that some people between the ages of 65 and 70 are reluctant to apply for old age assistance because they are too proud to do so.
It seems to me an invasion of private rights, Mr. Speaker, when officials of the federal government come and examine a person's assets and property as minutely as is essential under the administration of the Old Age Assistance Act. A very thorough investigation is required in order to guard against the possibility of abuse. However, there are people in this country who would prefer to go without old age assistance rather than to suffer that invasion of their private lives. This I can understand. Immediately it creates an anomaly, because some people are obtaining assistance and other people, equally entitled, are not. Both are taxpayers, but they are treated differently under the law because they are different types of people. The system of contributory pensions which must be introduced will eliminate these questions of individual philosophy and will provide, as a matter of right, a pension based on the earnings and contributions made by that individual throughout his working years.
If this can be accomplished it will reduce the existing anomalies. It will eliminate the necessity for investigations into the private lives of citizens. It will eliminate a situation in which, under the Old Age Pensions Act, millionaires and paupers receive the same payment, a payment which is completely inadequate to part of the population and completely unnecessary for another part of the population. I believe such a plan would be a considerable advantage to the portability of pensions and to the real security of Canadians when they reach the age of retirement.
However, Mr. Speaker, this type of plan has not been introduced. It seems, from what the government has said, that there is no possibility of it being introduced before a federal election is called. We have no assurance that it would be introduced even if the

speechtext:
I welcome this consideration given to old age assistance, in that it is a justification for those requests I made during a previous discussion on disabled people. In every sense old age assistance is a welfare scheme. Therefore this increase is of value, and the government is to be congratulated on having introduced it. It means that those who are not able to work any more will be able to pick up a little bit of money to help tide them over their difficulty.
I am in agreement with the previous speaker, who said this was not considered to be a substitute for work. It certainly is not, but we have reached the stage now at which we are all in agreement that we have to develop a national contributory and portable superannuation scheme which will take into consideration the advances in our society produced by the social changes that have taken place. We should face up to the fact that in a very short period of time there has been a total change from the dependency of elderly people on their families to a dependency on the state. By our changing technocracy many of these people have no alternative but to rely on assistance from the state.
The thinking of the Canadian people has changed from what it was in my grandfather's day, when it was accepted and demanded that the sons and daughters of elderly couples should be responsible for their parents' welfare. Now it is generally accepted that it is right to pay old age pensions to all the elderly people in the country. It is no longer considered as welfare but as a pension.
Years ago the Liberals used to refer to this as a national pension program. They considered it proper to provide national pensions. They considered this to be a far reaching step in providing national pensions, but I am surprised that few of our parliamentarians are willing to give credit to those unions which pioneered in this field and created a general acceptance for a national pension scheme. I am surprised that very few of them remember it was the unions which pioneered in this field long before the politicians entered it.
Looking at the record across the country we find that many plants have fairly respectable pension schemes and are only awaiting government assistance and leadership to introduce those plans into a national scheme


so they could be far more embracing than the present system under which they operate. For many years the C.C.F. party was in agreement that something should be done in that respect, and the plans that are being discussed today were outlined in this house by that party on numerous occasions. Now it is surprising to find there is very little difference of opinion in regard to those plans.
Should the political winds blow in their direction after the coming election, then it will only be a matter of one more election until a Conservative government gives a $75 pension. In fact, in the position they are in at present they are proposing that but, having been more farsighted, we saw this coming many years ago and we have been recommending $75 for a long time. In that connection it should be borne in mind that when we recommended $75 we knew there would be a limit eventually to the amount of money which governments could give under the so-called national scheme which has been in effect in Canada for a number of years. We knew that eventually consideration would have to be given to the establishment of a contributory section in the national pension scheme, and we suggested that this be done in a similar manner to the introduction of unemployment insurance.
This would mean that the federal government would administer the plan, as it does now, but it would also collect and retain the moneys that were collected on a national basis from all employees in industry and from the self-employed. These people would pay contributions to the federal government, which would hold the pension funds in trust for them.
We also believe the employers should be asked to make contributions. It is no longer possible for the average worker to accumulate money on his own for his retirement. I think, if we are to be fair, we do not expect workers or average citizens to save for their old age. If we did then we would be dishonest, because looking back over the years we can remember that a superannuation plan of 15 or 20 years ago created a maximum pension fund of $10,000, producing what would have been a fairly high standard of living in those days on $100 or $150 a month. However, that would prove totally inadequate in terms of purchasing power at present, and those who contributed to such plans now find they have only half the pensions they expected. Surely no country would intentionally do this to those who are seeking to provide their own superannuation programs.
Public thought in this country has increased to the extent that we now assume responsibility for our elderly citizens. We are now going to give increased attention to those

people who, because of their age, are no longer employable, and that is a factor which is changing very rapidly. There are many people in my own area seeking work at the age of 50, but they are not employable in terms of employers' interests. They apply for jobs, they are physically capable of doing them, but they are told they are too old. Indeed, in the mining field not only are they too old at 50 years but they are too old at 40, and some of the mines are raising their standards until prospective employees are told they are too old if they are nearing the age of 40.
The changes in technocracy and the changes in the employment picture are creating a demand for an immediate start on a contributory pension scheme, letting workers contribute from their earnings so that in many cases they will be granted an opportunity of working beyond what is now considered the acceptable age of employment. The fact that they would be contributing to a pension plan would mean their age would no longer be a factor, and would extend their employment.
This matter has been considered many times by governments in the hope that they would find a solution for the problem without getting involved in it themselves. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that a few years ago the Liberal government, through the then minister of national revenue, circulated a statement on principles and rules respecting pension plans for the purposes of income tax. They believed at that time that if income tax deductions were allowed on plans that were properly vested, then probably the labour unions themselves and employee-employer relationships would allow for a large segment of our country to be covered by this particular means.
This was not only considered by that government; it was considered by this government. In the Canada Gazette of July 18, 1959 this matter was again introduced by order in council and was again tried. In both cases this was unsuccessful in establishing what would be acceptable to industry, to employees and to the income tax department as a proper method of assessment.
I hope that for the sake of the old age pensioners, those on old age assistance, for social justice and the social picture in Canada, we do not reduce this matter of national pensions to an election issue and that we are serious when we say it will be referred to a committee. I hope that if an election is not anticipated immediately this matter will be referred to a committee of the house and that we will be given an opportunity to discuss the proposals this session, not in the light of an election but in the light of deliberations
Old Age Assistance Act in order that we may arrive at a pension plan which will be more acceptable and satisfactory to the Canadian people.

the second reading of Bill No. C-56, to amend the Blind Persons Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is designed, of course, to give effect to the proposed $10 increase in maximum benefits under the Blind Persons Act. The cost of this increase, as is the case with existing benefits, will be shared by the provincial and federal governments, the federal contribution amounting to 75 per cent of the total bill. As indicated in the resolution, it is also proposed to raise the allowable income ceiling by $180 a year in the case of an unmarried recipient and by $360 a year in the case of married couples. These new levels are higher than would be necessary to permit recipients to receive the full benefit of the higher maximum pension benefit. Our aim here is to encourage individual initiative by allowing recipients to have greater outside earnings without reduction of assistance.
The new levels also continue the tradition of higher income ceilings for recipients of blindness allowance as against recipients of old age assistance and disability allowances. Under present provisions, an unmarried recipient of blindness allowances without a dependant child or children is allowed to have $1,200 a year including allowances. This is to be increased to a total of $1,380 a year, made up of $780 by way of allowance and $600 by way of outside income. An unmarried recipient with a dependant child or children who is now allowed to have $1,680 including allowances will be permitted a- total of $1,860 a year. This will be made up of $780 by way of allowances and $1,080 by way of outside income.
A married couple where one spouse is blind is now allowed $1,980 a year in total income including benefit. This will be raised to $2,340 a year. Where one spouse is eligible for blindness allowance and the other for old age assistance, they will be able to receive as much as $1,560 a year by way of a benefit and have in addition $780 in outside income. If the blind spouse is receiving an allowance but the other spouse is not receiving a benefit, the maximum allowance payable is $780 a year and the outside income can be as much as $1,560 a year without reduction of benefit.
Where both spouses are blind, the couple is presently allowed $2,100 a year in total income including allowances. This amount is to be increased to $2,460. Where both spouses receive benefit, a maximum amount
Blind Persons Act
payable is $1,560 a year and in addition they can receive $900 in outside income. Where one spouse is eligible for the allowance and the other is not, the couple can receive $780 a year by way of allowances and $1,680 a year in outside income.
Since the Blind Persons Act is a joint federal-provincial undertaking, the comments I made with respect to the old age assistance bill are applicable to this amendment. That is, it will require the agreement of the provinces and territories to give effect to the proposed higher maximum benefits and higher income ceilings. As far as the federal government is concerned, the effective date of these changes will be February 1, 1962 and it is our hope that the provinces will find it possible to match this within their own jurisdiction. Copies of this bill have been sent to each province and my department stands ready to do everything possible to expedite the drawing up of new draft agreements embodying our present proposals.
Assuming that all ten provinces and the territories agree to the changes now before the house, it is estimated that the resulting increase in total outlays under the program will be of the order of $1.1 million in a 12 month period.
At the resolution stage, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) asked me how many persons were covered in the first year of the operation of pensions for the blind. For the fiscal year 1937-38 which was the year in question, the number of pensioners totalled 1,946. At that time the act covered blind persons aged 40 and over. On this basis the case load rose to 4,512 in 1938-39 and was running at between 5,000 and 7,000 over the next seven years. In 1947 the age requirement was lowered to 21 years and the number of recipients gradually climbed to slightly over 11,000 in 1950-51.
On December 31, 1951, the previous legislation ceased to operate, being replaced by the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act. Of the 11,335 blind recipients as at December 31, 1951, 3,212 were transferred to old age security and the remaining 8,123 became recipients under the Blind Persons Act. Since that time the case load has moved upward to the point where in December, 1961, 8,562 blind persons were receiving benefits.
I should point out that while significant, these figures do not of course present a complete picture of the number of blind persons in Canada. The most comprehensive source of information in this regard is the register maintained by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind which in 1961 reported a total of 24,117 blind persons in Canada. Of this

Blind Persons Act
number 9,102 were over 70 and presumed to be in receipt of old age security. At the same date, there were 8,642 recipients of blindness allowance and when the number benefiting under these two acts is added to the 351 war blinded and the 289 blind persons receiving workmen's compensation, it will be seen that a total of 18,384 persons were in receipt of benefits of one kind or another. This means that about 76 per cent of the number of blind persons registered with the Canadian National Institute for the Blind were receiving benefit under government programs.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate also requested a general picture of blindness in Canada. The figures reported by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind indicate a slow but steady increase in the prevalence of blindness in Canada over the past 15 years. This apparent increase is due in part to a more comprehensive reporting of blindness. However, with the increase in life span, more citizens reach the older age groups in which blindness due to glaucoma, cataracts and degenerating conditions occurs more frequently. Nearly half of the total number of registered blind are over 65, and over one third of the total are over 70 years of age.
As the house is aware, my department has taken an active interest in the prevention, treatment and rehabilitation of blind persons. In co-operation with nine of the provincial governments, we conduct a program to provide operations for the restoration of sight to recipients of blindness allowances. Alberta does not participate in the treatment program, having its own plan in this regard. The great majority of these operations are done for the removal of cataracts. However, in recent years corneal transplants have been performed with increasing frequency, and in the past two years this type of surgery was carried out in eight per cent of the cases receiving treatment. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that we carry out the treatment program in cooperation with nine of the provinces. This is handled through the blindness control division of the health branch of my department, and we participate to the extent of 75 per cent of the cost.
In the past fiscal year 105 persons were provided with treatment under this program. The great majority of persons accepting treatment were in the group of approximately 800 citizens who were granted blindness allowances in the course of the year and who were, for the most part, persons whose blindness was of relatively recent development.
Since the inception of the treatment program in 1948, a total of 731 persons had been treated by the end of the past fiscal year. Of these, 562 or 77 per cent, had their sight

restored to the extent that they were no longer blind, and the majority of the remaining 23 per cent benefited by varying degrees of improvement in guiding vision. The house can be sure that my department will continue to do everything possible to reduce the toll taken by blindness in Canada. Present provisions will be carried forward and new avenues will be explored wherever they hold out hope for further progress.

I wish to make some criticisms at this time. I trust the minister will not consider that I am criticizing his department because what applies there now probably applied before. I have had considerable experience over the years with people attempting to qualify for disability pensions. I believe some confusion exists with respect to the interpretation of the words "totally and permanently disabled".
The minister explained today that in Ottawa from time to time conferences are held of doctors of provincial boards, to give consideration to the various conditions that might cause total and permanent disability. Probably such conferences were held during the tenure of office of the previous minister.
Yesterday the hon. member for Timiskam-ing (Mr. Peters) said that he thought a person with a disability might qualify in one province while another individual with the same condition living in another province might be denied the pension. I believe that this could happen. Confusion exists in the minds of medical men largely because they do not understand what constitutes a total and permanent disability under this act.
If a person has advanced arthritis and is confined to a wheelchair it is usually not difficult for him to qualify for the pension. However, there are many other conditions which are just as disabling in terms of the individual making a living and the victims of these conditions frequently find it difficult to qualify for a pension under the act.
I can think of patients of my own in the past who were unable to qualify for the pension. I can think of mental and psychological conditions which are disabling in terms of the individual earning a livelihood. I know of people with schizophrenia whose condition does not warrant their being hospitalized but who are unable to earn a living. They have such negative personalities they could not stick with a job for more than an hour and certainly they require direction. These people cannot earn a living.
I have a vivid recollection of a woman who was so psychologically upset she could not earn a livelihood. After a period of hospitalization she would appear to be well but when discharged she would lapse back to her previous condition.
Not many people who suffer from a condition such as premature aging as a result of

arteriosclerosis are able to quality for a pension under the act. Let us take coronary disease of the heart as another example. I have seen a patient as young as age 18 die of this disease. How many in their thirties or forties could qualify for a pension even if disabled to the extent that they were not able to walk very much on the level because of heart disease?
There are certain diseases which have remissions. I think of leukemia, for example. A person applying for a pension under the act during a period of remission would certainly have no chance of qualifying because he would look so well. The situation would be much improved if the experts would always accept the true report sent in by the doctor, but I have found that is not always the case. But differences of opinion would naturally arise.
There are a number of disabling conditions in respect of which a doctor cannot honestly put his signature on paper and say that the patient is permanently disabled. There are a number of diseases that lead to a fatal termination in the majority of cases but in a few other cases the victims do recover for a time. We know this is true in some cases of cancer, cirrhosis of the liver and others. Few recover but their health improves so they can work for a time. Unless a doctor is able to say they are totally and permanently disabled these people do not qualify under the act. Most of these people are permanently disabled within the meaning of the regulations, in the final result, but can any doctor say at the beginning they are permanently disabled under the act?

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of bringing forward this measure is that it contains certain amendments which will remove anomalies that have persisted for a number of years, about which a great many hon. members of the present parliament and earlier parliaments have spoken. It has therefore seemed advisable to clear away some of these things which require attention and recognize certain groups which served during warfare under difficult and dangerous conditions but which have not received the same attention as veterans.
The difficulty over the years has been with regard to the definition of the word "veteran", which we are not changing in the amendments; but because of the definition of the word "veteran" people who were not enlisted and in uniform in the various categories which I will mention shortly have not been eligible for some of the benefits under the veterans charter. The intention of the amendments about to be proposed is to bring these categories, not under the War Veterans

Allowance Act but to make available to them the assistance that is provided to veterans under that act. I have a prepared statement which I think will put on the record as it summarizes rather carefully the various amendments which we have in mind.
