speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING PAYMENTS TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
The Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act was passed in 1946 to provide pensions to members of a number of civilian groups who became disabled while furthering the national war effort and to the dependants of those who lost their lives as a direct result of enemy action. The word "allowances" in the title has so far referred to detention allowances which were paid to merchant seamen if they were detained or imprisoned by another country. The allowances compensated for the loss of wages suffered because of detention. The act as it is at present is administered by the Canadian pension commission.
The amendment proposed by the bill is to add a new section to the act to permit the payment of allowances in amounts similar to war veterans allowances and under similar conditions of financial need or disability. The contribution of the members of these groups to the war effort was praiseworthy and in many instances brought sacrifices in addition to disabilities involving financial loss and family hardship through separation and other strains as well as many discomforts and privations. It thus seems appropriate that where these civilians are unable to follow a reasonably gainful occupation and have very limited resources, they should be assisted in order that they may enjoy a modest but secure income as a token of the national appreciation of their contribution to the war effort.
Although it is necessary to speak of them using the term "civilians" rather than "veterans", that is not because those of us who are veterans, in addition to others, do not recognize that their contribution was in many instances greater than that which we ourselves made during wartime. I would refer particularly to the men in the merchant marine who have been recognized in many other ways but who have not heretofore been given the privileges which pertain to veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act. I have stated before in this house how much we owe to these men and again I pay a tribute to the men of the merchant marine in particular, not singling them out especially from the other groups which will be mentioned later, but referring to them because I have always had a great admiration for the merchant marine. These men undertook, voluntarily, jobs for which I, for one, might have volunteered only under extremely pressing

circumstances; I have often thought that if I had been asked during wartime to take a job as a merchant seaman I would have paused to think about it on more than one occasion. Each service sometimes wonders how the other service is managed in wartime, and as just an ordinary soldier I often wondered about the men of the merchant marine.
The groups to whom it is proposed that allowances be made available are:
1.	World war I. The Canadian merchant marine and those Canadians who served in the merchant services of the allies.
There were 39 merchant ships of Canadian registry during world war I, and a number of Newfoundland registry. A small number of Canadians served in British and allied merchant shipping. It is estimated that there were about 5,000 merchant seamen who served in all these ships. Most seamen served in dangerous waters. We cannot determine accurately the number of these who survive, but a careful estimate indicates that only a few hundred seamen and widows are now alive.
The annual cost is estimated at about $105,000. As this group is now decreasing because of advancing age the cost will drop quickly.
We are hopeful that although official records of service will in most cases be nonexistent, proofs of service at sea will be available through the discharge books of the seamen, authorization for medals or other contemporary records.
2.	World war II. The Canadian merchant marine and those Canadians who served with Canada's allies on certified non-Canadian ships.
There were 194 merchant ships of Canadian registry and a number of Newfoundland registry. Canadian seamen served in many certified non-Canadian ships including a number who served under an agreement with the British admiralty, known as a T-124 agreement which applied tq< service on such ships as armed merchant cruisers and rescue tugs. From the records of these world war II groups there should be little difficulty in establishing proof of service. It is estimated that there are now about 20,000 survivors of all these groups including widows and orphan children and that about 400 would now qualify for allowances on the basis of service eligibility consisting of at least six months spent at sea during the war including at least one voyage through dangerous waters, or the award of a pension or a detention allowance under this act.
The estimated present annual cost of allowances to this group is $500,000.
Civilian War Pensions
3.	World war II. Corps of (civilian) Canadian firefighters for service in the United Kingdom.
This corps was organized in Canada for service in Britain to assist the national fire service in combating fires caused by enemy air raids. Members were required to serve for the duration of the war or as long thereafter as necessary. Of the 422 firefighters who enrolled in the corps, 408 served in Britain and had all arrived there by December, 1942. The average length of service for those who proceeded overseas was two years and nine months. Those who served for at least six months in Britain during the hostilities in Europe received the defence of Britain medal. Complete service records of this corps are available. It is proposed that service eligibility for allowances will require a continuous period of at least six months spent in Britain prior to May 9, 1945 or the award of a pension under this act, and that the widows and orphan children of deceased members who saw such service be also eligible.
The estimated annual cost is $12,000.
4.	World war I. Voluntary aid detachment.
This detachment was selected by the St.
John Ambulance Brigade and sent to Britain to assist the Women's V.A.D. department of the British Red Cross. They served in imperial hospitals in Britain and on the continent, having proceeded overseas between September 1916 and September 1918. Of the total of 360 who proceeded overseas 54, including 12 from Newfoundland, served on the continent of Europe and received the Victory Medal and the General Service Medal. Nominal rolls are available. The bill provides that members of this detachment and the orphan children of deceased members be eligible for allowances provided that before November 12, 1918 they served on the continent or at least 365 days in Britain including sailing time from Canada and on return during the period of hostilities or, alternatively, were pensioned under this act.
5.	World war II. Overseas welfare workers.
This was a group of women who served
overseas under the auspices of the Canadian Red Cross society, the St. John ambulance brigade and the Scottish ministry of health. They served in various capacities such as nursing aids, ambulance drivers and welfare workers. Some served as orthopaedic nurses with the Scottish ministry of health. The first women left Canada in January, 1943. The majority served in Britain only although some served in the Mediterranean theatre and others in France and Belgium. Virtually complete records are available. There were 861 workers who left Canada for service

It is proposed that, as these workers served in Britain and on the continent under hazardous conditions, they and the orphan children of deceased workers, be eligible for allowances provided they served overseas for a continuous period of at least six months or are pensioned under this act. The annual cost would be very small.
6.	World war II. Canadian civilian air crew of the Royal Air Force transport command.
These men were first employed in 1940 as civilians to fly bombers and other aircraft across the Atlantic. In 1941 the organization was taken over by the R.A.F. transport command. At the conclusion of hostilities there were 269 Canadian survivors of this group. Complete records are available. The members suffered a fatal casualty rate of 20 per cent. It is proposed that those who served as air crew for at least six months during the war and who made at least one ocean crossing and the widows and orphan children of deceased members be eligible for allowances. The annual cost would be very small.
7.	World war II. Newfoundland overseas forestry unit.
This group was recruited in Newfoundland at the request of the British government. The earlier contracts were for six months only but subsequent contracts were for the duration of the war. They were engaged in the cutting of pit props for coal mines, an activity vital to the war economy. They served mostly in Scotland. Of the total of 3,680 who went overseas about 3,100 remained as civilians as some of the first group joined the forces. The group suffered about 30 fatal accidents and 335 were repatriated on medical grounds. Records are virtually complete. It is proposed that the members of this unit who contracted to serve with the unit for the duration of the war and who served in Britain for at least six months and the widows and orphan children of deceased members with this service be eligible for allowances. The present annual cost is estimated at $60,000.
The above proposals to permit the payment of allowances to the survivors and surviving dependants of the members of the above groups are contained in a new part to be added to this act as part XI. Parts I to X will, as before, continue to be adjudicated and administered by the Canadian pension commission. The adjudication and the administrative duties brought about by the new part XI will become the responsibility of the war veterans allowance board and the W.V.A. district authorities. The authority for these duties is now contained in the War Veterans Allowance Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING PAYMENTS TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the minister and the government for introducing this resolution. It states a principle with which we are in full accord and which we heartily endorse. For some time we in this party have advocated that pensions be given to members of the merchant navy, the rescue tug service commonly known as the T-124 group, the firefighters and members of the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit. We are glad to see that the valuable services rendered to our country by these and other groups in two world wars are now being recognized.
I said we fully support the principle of this resolution but we have no way of knowing how widely the principle will be applied until we see the bill. Until the legislation is before us we cannot determine for ourselves the conditions under which these people will become eligible for pensions nor will we be in a position to determine its actual usefulness.
Judging from the figure given by the minister with respect to the cost of pensions for the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit it seems to me the conditions are going to be very stringent indeed. If the cost is going to be only $60,000 it may be calculated that at $1,000 for each individual the government does not expect more than 60 members of the unit to qualify this year.
Although I endorse the principle I must place on record my personal disappointment at the vehicle chosen by the government for applying the principle. I had hoped that the method adopted would have been by amending the veterans charter so that these groups could be accorded the same treatment we accord other veterans. It seems to me it would have been a very simple matter to amend the definition of a veteran in such a way that these groups could be included. The fact that this has not been done amounts to denying these people the status of veterans. While we are assisting them in one breath, in the next breath we are saying that we do not regard them as veterans.
I appreciate what the minister said about the merchant navy. He knows I share the admiration he expressed for the services they rendered during the war. Their services were just as vital and necessary to the winning of the war as those rendered by any other branch of the armed services. Without the merchant navy there would have been no food for our troops or our allies in Britain, no fuel to run our tanks and motor vehicles, no ammunition and no arms. If you take that into consideration you will conclude we could not have won the war without the contribution of the merchant navy.
The minister said the amendments envisaged payment to these groups somewhat along

the lines of the war veterans allowance. That allowance is paid to veterans on reaching age 60 without the requirement of a medical examination. We call it the burnt out pension. It is awarded on the assumption- whether true or false I am not prepared to say-that the hardships undergone by those men in carrying out their duties had an effect on their physical condition that would not have been experienced had they remained in civilian life and that served to pre-age them by ten years. If that is true with respect to the armed services, I am sure it is doubly true with respect to members of the merchant navy.
The minister said he would not like to be in the position of a merchant seaman, and I would not either, sitting on a fuel tanker which might be blown up and catch fire at any minute in mid-Atlantic, or sitting on a munition ship which would need only one shell to blow everyone to kingdom come, being cramped in small quarters with people suffering from tuberculosis and other ailments or floating about in the ocean for hours on end waiting to be picked up. Certainly if any conditions would create preaging I would think that those I have just mentioned would lead to that result.
We are glad to see that these benefits are being extended to the other groups mentioned by the minister. I will not take the time to list them all. We acknowledge their services too, but what disturbs me is that the government, having chosen to go so far, has stopped short of going just a little bit farther and granting to these people the status of veterans. What we see here is that all a person needs to do to be a veteran is to put on a uniform. I have known people who put on a uniform, landed in France, spent a day or two there, broke a leg and were transported back to blighty. Such a man is a veteran though he never got into action. He never got near the front line but he is a veteran. On the other hand, the poor merchant navy man who was torpedoed, floated for hours in the ocean and was lucky to escape with his life is not a veteran. I think this omission is going to be a severe disappointment to the members of the merchant navy.
I see that my time is running out and I will merely pass over the other groups by saying that I welcome this recognition of their services because I want to take a minute or two to refer to the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit. In respect of this group this is special legislation because it will not apply to any other foresters or any other forestry unit except those in Newfoundland, and in Newfoundland only to those who served in world war II.
Civilian War Pensions
Here again we have identical conditions involving the summoning to service of these people by the British government, a vital service so important that they were frozen in their occupation and not allowed to join the other services even though many of them wished to do so. In addition to their forestry service, some of them served in the home guard in the British Isles and manned guns and performed other defence duties in Britain.
But the thing I want to point out to the minister about this legislation is that it is drawing a distinction between Newfoundland forestry units who served in world war I and those who served in world war II, because the Newfoundland foresters who served in world war I are veterans. They are recognized as veterans and are receiving benefits today under the veterans charter. Yet we are saying to those who served in world war II and performed exactly identical services that they are not veterans.
What is the difference, Mr. Chairman? The only difference is that those who served in world war I wore uniforms and those who served in world war II did not because they were recruited under different conditions and in such an urgent way. At that time Newfoundland did not have responsible government but was governed by a commission with headquarters in Britain. The head of the government was really the colonial secretary in London and he laid down what was or was not to be done. If we had been a free people at that time instead of being governed by what was actually a dictatorship-it may have been a benevolent one but nevertheless it was still a dictatorship because the people had no say in their government-the Newfoundland people would have seen to it that the Newfoundland foresters of world war II were treated in exactly the same way as those who served in the same capacity in world war I.
The people of Newfoundland did not have a voice in the government of their country and it would have been a nice gesture if in bringing in this legislation the government had rectified the omission and put the foresters of world war II on exactly the same footing as those of world war I. We now have in Newfoundland two classes of foresters, those who served in world war I and are veterans and entitled to benefits under the veterans charter and those who served in world war II who are not veterans and not entitled to benefits under the charter but who are now being brought under the civilian pensions act.
That is not what I wanted, that is not what they wanted, that is not what the Canadian Legion wanted. The Legion made it very clear in its submissions to the government

Railway Act
and to the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs in 1960 and 1961 and on other occasions that it was recommending that these groups should be brought in under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Even at this late date I would ask the minister to reconsider this whole matter and try to wipe out the anomalies which he said in his opening remarks this legislation is intended to remove.

After the abandonment of the line of railway, the railway company erected fences or barriers at each end of the abandoned right of way, but these erections have from time to time been destroyed or have fallen out of repair, and the public has used the right of way to some extent as an ordinary road for travel. As a consequence of the lack of fencing the applicants claim that they have been seriously damaged in respect of their farm which lies upon both sides of the railway right of way. They complain that trespassers and cattle get upon their property from time to time from the railway right of way and that there are no fences upon the right of way to prevent their so doing, and that under present circumstances they have suffered a great deal of damage and inconvenience in respect of their farm property and farm operations.
The application was heard in the city of Toronto on November 3, 1936, in the presence of the applicants and their counsel, and also in the presence of counsel for the railway company. At the conclusion of the hearing it was suggested that the railway company might at slight expense erect permanent barriers at each end of its abandoned line of railway where it crosses applicants' property, which would effectually stop trespassing and travel upon its former railway line in the vicinity of applicants' farm. Counsel for the railway company agreed to this suggestion and stated that the railway company would be willing to erect suitable barriers for such purpose at the above points, and would also erect and maintain proper signs or notices warning persons against trespassing and that the railway company would endeavour in any reasonable way to prosecute trespassers should the practice continue.
It is to be noted that the requirement for fencing is that the company shall erect and maintain fences upon the railway (section 274 of the Railway Act). Where abandonment of operation has been authorized and has taken place, the right of way through which the railway is operated ceases to be used for railway purposes and is held by the company, not as part of its railway qua railway company, but in the same way as land is held by private individuals, subject to any provincial or municipal laws which may be in force in the particular district.
It is to be further noted that the principal, if not the sole, reason for the fencing requirement in the Railway Act is to prevent cattle from getting upon railway lands and being killed or injured by railway operations. Where complete abandonment of a line of railway takes place, the necessity for fencing the line largely disappears, and the section does not apply. For these reasons the board, in my opinion, has no authority under the terms of the Railway Act to order the railway company to maintain fences upon the sides of its right of way under the circumstances which pertain in the present application. It is, of course, open to the applicants, if they so desire, to seek whatever remedy in respect of fencing may be available under the provisions of the provincial laws.
When it was pointed out to the applicants at the hearing that the board lacked jurisdiction to make an order such as the applicants desired, they were disposed to accept the suggestion above set out in regard to the erection of barriers by the railway company at each end of the abandoned right of way, where the same crosses the farm property of applicants. It may be that under all the circumstances it would be better to erect these barriers at the points where the right of way intersects the highways nearest to the property of the applicants. The erection of barriers at the

highway intersections might effectually put a stop to the trespassing of which the applicants complain.
An order will, therefore, be issued in the above terms providing for the erection and maintenance of the said barriers and the notices to trespassers as above mentioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take advantage of this opportunity to say a few words in

support of the bill of my colleague from Middlesex West who comes from my neighbouring municipality and constituency.
This bill is intended to correct a situation which is, in my opinion also, an injustice caused in connection with the abandonment of railway rights of way. I approve and consider most commendable the purpose which is written in the bill itself. If I may quote that purpose again, it is this:
The purpose of this bill is to make legislatively certain that the board of transport commissioners has authority to order railway companies to so maintain abandoned lines of railway as to prevent damages to the rights of persons or the interest of the public.
To my mind that is a most commendable purpose. Wherever such instances of abandonment take place they are almost certain to cause difficulties and inconveniences which are not of the making of the individuals affected. Since these things are not of the making of the individuals, and in the main have not been requested by the individual property owners but have been carried out to serve the public generally, it does not seem fair that the individual should be faced with the excessive costs that are the results of such abandonments taking place.
As I said, I am a neighbouring representative of my colleague who has just spoken and I believe I am affected in about the same way in that this railway which has been abandoned in our area crosses through the territory that I have the privilege and honour to represent.
The main cause of complaint that has come to me in this regard has been in connection with fencing. A number of individual property owners have asked me to make representations to the powers that be, because they have not been able to obtain what they consider to be a fair and equitable arrangement for the maintaining of the fences that are affecting them.
There are also other matters, such as grading-which has been mentioned by my colleague-drainage, bridges and culverts, and so on. I have had occasion to intercede on behalf of these people I have mentioned and I have been told that as a result of the abandonment of these railway lines the property now falls into the same position as that of any other ratepayer adjoining these properties, as far as the law is concerned. This law, as perhaps most hon. members know, provides that wherever fencing is required the people affected have the right to go to their municipal representatives and ask them to make a fence viewer's award in a case where they cannot agree as to the relative proportions of the cost of maintaining these fences.
Railway Act
As hon. members can readily understand, a rail line requires two fences in order to protect it. In the case where a rail line cuts a farm property it is necessary to maintain two additional fences across that property in order to protect the cattle or livestock, whatever they may be, from the hazards and dangers of the railway. Where the rail line has ceased to function it means that the farmer must pay the cost of one complete fence across his property which in the first place is cut in two, and in regard to which he has no access to the back. He must maintain a fence through it in order to protect his cattle from getting out and getting into trouble. To my mind the cost involved is prohibitive for him because I presume the value of the land involved-which would only be a few acres at the most-would in some cases not be equal to the value of the fence.
I should also like to say a few words about the question of drainage. I believe that our laws, particularly in Ontario, provide that wherever one interferes with the free flow of water one automatically becomes responsible for carrying his share of the cost of taking that water to a place where it will do no damage to lands or roads. In the case where a grade is built up or a hill is cut down, it has the effect of either increasing the flow of water beyond that which nature would allow, or it has the opposite effect of cutting off the free flow of water so that it cannot be carried to a point where it will do no damage to lands or roads.
The result is that the farmer must suffer additional damage as a result of water that is artificially cut off from its natural flow. Where culverts are taken out, naturally they will erode and fill in. This will cause a natural dam because there would have been a grade built by the railway in order to build up its line to the place where it would give the best service.
I do not think I am in a position to stress any of the other things which have been mentioned and which the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) has covered very fully. I will conclude by saying that I agree with the bill and I should like to see authority vested in the board of transport commissioners so they would be able to order that lines shall be maintained where there has been an abandonment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-7 which we are now considering most certainly has our sympathy. In principle it goes far deeper than even the actual wording of the bill. The title of the bill is an act to amend the Railway Act

Railway Act
(abandonment). The foremost principles outlined therein are to the effect that the company may abandon the operation of any line of railway with the approval of the board and upon such terms and conditions subsequent as the board from time to time may by order provide. The basic concept of the bill is that there shall be no abandonment until or unless the company has complied with any order by the board to carry out remedial measures in the way of fencing, gates, cattle-guards, weed control, drainage works, demolition and so on.
What is outlined here is certainly important. We should like to congratulate the hon. member for having introduced this bill because of the basic, underlying, important, fundamental principle which is directly and indirectly conveyed in the measure, that is, the question of the abandonment of railway lines and the effect of so doing upon the public in general, upon farmers and upon industry. That is why we feel this bill is important. I think we are too prone to forget the basis upon which the transcontinental railways of Canada were built. The primary object was to link Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific in order to develop the economy of our country. To make this possible not only were hundreds of millions of dollars granted through the medium of the federal government but other considerations were forthcoming by way of grants of land and mineral resources which over the years have amounted to billions of dollars. The idea was to open Canada for development and, in addition, to give service to the Canadian people in perpetuity because of the billions which had been granted to the companies in cash or resources.
In the last few years, however, applications have been made from time to time to the board of transport commissioners for the abandonment of lines which, in the estimation of the railway companies, can no longer be operated at a profit. That, I say, is the fundamental issue which is before us now because of this bill. It affects all Canada. It affects us in the province of British Columbia. I have particularly in mind the Kettle valley line which is a major transportation system in our province going from Vancouver through the cities of Penticton, Castlegar, Trail, Nelson and Fernie to Lethbridge. Although this line is not completely abandoned it is partly abandoned to the extent that as far as service to the public is concerned in all the cities I have named it is basically operated only for one reason and that is the convenience of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company for freight transfer and, of course, the majority stockholder in that company is the Canadian Pacific Railway. So we are facing not

only the question of abandonment but of the partial abandonment of service to the people of Canada who have contributed so much of their God-given resources and hard cash to these companies over the years. There is no question that the hon. member who moved this bill and the speaker who preceded me were completely correct in saying that now, before it is too late, steps must be taken to protect the public.
We think the introduction of this bill will serve to draw the attention of the government and of the board of transport commissioners to the need, when any application is made for the abandonment of rail lines, of consideration being given to those who have established themselves, whether on farms or in industry, for time during which to make transportation readjustments and for adequate and fair compensation for any increased costs which they may have to incur because of the abandonment of the lines. Without going into great detail I should like to say that as far as this group is concerned, we ask, in supporting this Bill No. C-7, that some thought be given by the board of transport commissioners to the public service which is being provided to our people and to the obligation which the railways owe to them because of past gifts. We ask that when any request is made for abandonment the transportation commissioners should keep in mind that agreement to abandon must be on terms providing that new types of transportation have been installed so as to maintain those whose work or service would be disrupted because of abandonment. Also, I hope the board will bear in mind the extra cost which may have to be incurred by industrialists and farmers affected by abandonment, and that in view of this extra cost the board will order compensation to be paid over whatever period of time may seem necessary. This is an important matter of vital principle which should be attended to immediately by the government and by the board of transport commissioners both for the protection of our economy and also of those who have invested their physical and mental labour or money in projects because of the railway services which previously existed. In other words, there must be a time period ordered by the board of transport commissioners during which other means of transportation may be established, and provision made for compensation to those who incur increased cost in getting their products to the markets of the world.

speechtext:
I am pleased to give my support to this bill in the name of the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas). I am also pleased that the hon.

member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has indicated the support of his party for this measure. I think the amendment is important in view of the fact that the board of transport commissioners is being asked by the two major railways in Canada for permission to discontinue a number of branch lines which, in the opinion of the railways, have become uneconomic.
Within the past week the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented a brief to the Prime Minister and the cabinet. They are concerned in that brief with the abandonment of railway lines in Canada. I wish to quote some comments from their brief on this subject:
However, on two major points of policy we are quite clear. The first concerns abandonment of branch lines. Conceding that there will and should be abandonment of a considerable number of branch lines over the next number of years, we would emphasize as strongly as possible that branch line abandonment, especially in the grain economy of western Canada but in many other cases also, can have severe repercussions on business using these lines and on farmers. The central need in this connection is to avoid ill-considered, overhasty, and unco-ordinated programs of branch line abandonment.
Our recommendation is that the government and board of transport commissioners should insist that before further abandonment is proceeded with a long range plan for abandonment and relocation of displaced elevator and other facilities should be developed which embraces in one plan the operations of both railways. It should insist also on a reasonable notice of perhaps five years to be given before abandonment. The government should develop, in advance of co-operating in a program of branch line abandonment, adequate policies with respect to depreciation allowances on needed new facilities, on facilities which will require to be abandoned, and where necessary for recovery of costs of investment on abandoned branches. Given such an orderly, over-all plan, adequate consultation with producers and other interested parties on the plan, and necessary subsidiary tax and compensation policies, it should be possible for constructive progress to be made with fairness to all concerned.
In the province of Ontario, the federation of agriculture has established a land acquisition committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Jack Ferguson, past president of the Ontario federation of agriculture. For a number of years this committee has been engaged in making an intensive study and survey of the effects on farm property of power lines, pipe lines, railroads and other public services. I understand this committee has gone on record as saying that action be taken similar to that recommended in the proposal of the hon. member for Middlesex West.
At the present time, the Ontario federation of agriculture along with the county branches in Lambton, Middlesex and Elgin have formed a joint committee and are or will be holding meetings or circulating petitions among those persons involved to gain their views on the abandonment of the New York Central line
Railway Act
through these three counties. I refer to the line running from St. Thomas known as the Saint Clair line. The abandonment of railway lines is always of concern to county weed inspectors and their views will also be considered.
I offer for consideration the following suggestion. After a railway line has been discontinued for a certain period of time-we might use the period of five years, for example -and the tracks removed, the land would revert to the original deed. It would then become the responsibility of the now present owner to keep it fenced and to control the weeds. In case of dispute over line fences they would then come, in this province, under the Ontario line fence act and be subject to a decision rendered by the fence viewers of the local municipality.
I personally have recollection of a railroad line in the riding of Elgin being discontinued, but of course this took place approximately 40 years ago. The line at that time was known as the London and Port Stanley Traction Company. It was an electric railway handling mainly passengers and express. I do not think the line had to discontinue by reason of competition from motor cars and trucks; rather, it was as a result of competition from a competitive electric railroad serving the same area. When the tracks were removed the people in the area were given the opportunity to remove the ballast along the right of way for use in building up their own roadways or drives. Eventually the land reverted to the original owners and in a few years time the right of way was levelled and became once again productive, agricultural land. Much of this line ran along what is now No. 4 highway. The Ontario department of highways took over the abandoned line when the highway was widened.
In my estimation Bill No. 7 as introduced by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) is very timely. I hope it receives not only favourable consideration by hon. members of this house but, as well, support from the cabinet and the board of transport commissioners.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF ABANDONED LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as was mentioned by the previous speaker in his closing remarks this bill is certainly timely, particularly in relation to my constituency. A number of branch lines have been abandoned in the last 25 years and the people in my area are concerned over the fact that we might again be faced with further rail line abandonment. In fact the railroads are now applying for permission to abandon a short stretch of railway in the area. Bill No. C-7 is therefore of vital interest to my constituency.

Railway Act
Under present conditions a railway must apply for permission to abandon a line but the board of transport commissioners imposes no qualifications with respect to abandonment. In other words, once permission is granted the railway may remove itself from the picture as rapidly as it can, leaving behind as little mess as possible, but with no regard for the people affected. The railways are free to take that course if they wish.
When it is found necessary to abandon a line considerable hardship is imposed on the owners of property located along the railway and particularly property owners such as the owners of small businesses in communities or small towns. It is true that some businesses are not today patronizing the railways as much as they should be. However, the loss of a railway greatly affects a small community.
Elevator companies are also vastly affected by rail line abandonment. In the last five or six years elevator companies have taken the position of stating that the larger the elevator, the cheaper costs of operating the elevator and handling grain. They have produced statistics showing that an elevator with a capacity of 100,000 bushels can handle grain at half the cost of an elevator with a capacity of 25,000 or 30,000 bushels. This may be true, but certainly if a rail line is abandoned you have an elevator left which is merely salvage. As soon as it was empty I imagine it would be torn down. The elevator companies stand to lose a considerable amount in any abandonment of a rail line, but I am not really concerned about the position of the elevator companies.
The aspect at which I think the board of transport commissioners should take a serious look is the greater hardship and difficulty people will have in getting their products to market and the losses people will suffer because of property devaluation. Many persons have built homes in these small towns in the hope that the towns will continue to flourish and that they will be able to spend the rest of their days there; but they find that these towns are slowly fading away. If the railway line is abandoned and the tracks are pulled up, then sooner or later businesses will leave these towns and the people will either have to move to another town or continue to live in a ghost town.
This is the part of the problem that concerns me, and I think that the railways should bear some responsibility in this regard. As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) mentioned, this bill should serve to bring this problem to the attention of the cabinet and the board of transport commissioners. I think it should also serve to bring the problem to the forefront so far as the

railway companies are concerned and in my view they should give the whole matter very serious consideration because in western Canada particularly towns sprung up as a result of the urging of the railway companies.
The railway companies bought land and laid out town sites. In many cases they sold lots to businessmen who wanted to establish businesses. They encouraged men to invest their life savings in these towns along the railway lines, and if these lines are abandoned the railway should share some responsibility for the loss these people will suffer and the greater hardships that farmers, mines and so on will face in getting their products to market.
When one of the railways applies to the board of transport commissioners for permission to abandon a railway line, certainly the board must look into the problem to ascertain how many people are affected, how much business is affected, how grain handling facilities will be affected and how much of a loss the railway is suffering in its operation of the line. Then the board must weigh the one against the other. When the board is making its very thorough investigation with regard to the loss suffered by the railway and the potential loss to business people, farmers, tradesmen and workers in the area, surely it should not be too much to expect it to impose regulations on the railway as to how the abandonment should take place and who should be compensated for what. This only seems right, and perhaps in most cases the board would do this; but as I understand the act the railways could not be forced to follow such policy or regulations outlined by the board of transport commissioners.
I know that a great deal of hardship could be experienced as a result of the abandonment of certain rail lines. It would cause workers who derive their livelihood from the railways to change their occupation. It is a common statement for the railways to make that they will make room for such people elsewhere in the system, but we are all aware of the bumping that takes place on the railways and somebody down the line gets bumped out of a job. This is the sort of thing that could happen to people actually concerned in the operating of the railway lines. Then there are the people whose property will perhaps go right down to nil in value because of the loss of the railway line passing their property. I think this will be the actual result in the case of a great many towns but it will take a number of years for it to happen. I am certain that will be the result in many small places.
Very few small places in western Canada will continue to exist without a railway line running through them. Farmers will have to

haul grain a greater distance to another elevator on another track so that the grain can be moved to the lakehead or to the west coast for shipment. This will undoubtedly mean greater cost which will have to be borne by the farmer who has to get his grain to market. It is quite clear that the board has to rule on abandonment and I think it should also rule on how abandonment will take place and how compensation will be paid. Certainly the railways should accept their responsibility and realize that they owe some compensation to those people who suffer by reason of the abandonment of a rail line.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire whether on Monday we will go back to the speech from the throne and, if not, what the business for that day and subsequent days will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:

The second item will be the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport concerning a railway line at Whitecourt, Alberta; third, second reading of Bill No. C-48, respecting a railway line at Chisel lake, Manitoba; fourth, the resolution in the name of the Minister of
Business of the House
Transport which appears in Votes and Proceedings for yesterday and deals with a proposed railway line in the Gaspe peninsula.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out to the house leader that we gave an undertaking to expedite one of the measures on the order paper. speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Expediting any of the business I have announced would be met with pleasure on this side of the house and we could then get back to the speech from the throne.
